title: Neutralisation and the equivalence point
body: An acid gives hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water, and a base like sodium hydroxide gives hydroxide ions (OH⁻). When they meet, they join up to make water: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

Neutralisation is a reaction, not just mixing. Each drop of base uses up some of the acid's H⁺ ions, but the solution stays acidic until they have all been used up. For 25 mL of 0.1 M hydrochloric acid, that takes exactly 25 mL of 0.1 M sodium hydroxide.

Right at that point, the equivalence point, the solution is neutral: pH 7. A few more drops leave spare OH⁻ ions, so the pH shoots up and the solution turns basic. That sudden jump is why chemists add the last few drops so carefully.
realWorld: Farmers spread lime, a base, on soil that has become too acidic, and antacids neutralise extra stomach acid. In both cases the amount matters: too much base overshoots and makes things basic.
